lead.en: West Africa masters iron and sculpts in terracotta

summary.en: The Nok culture emerged in what is now Nigeria, renowned for its expressive terracotta sculptures. Its people were among the first in West Africa to smelt iron.

lead.en: Biblical tradition: birth of a city sacred to three faiths

summary.en: According to biblical tradition, King David captured Jerusalem from the Jebusites and made it the capital of a united kingdom of Israel. The City of David became the sacred centre of Judaism and later of Christianity and Islam.

lead.en: Bronze drums of ancient Vietnam spread across Southeast Asia

summary.en: This Bronze Age culture of the Red River and Ma valleys lasted from about 1000 BC to the start of the Common Era. Its emblem is the great bronze drum decorated with boats, houses, birds and warriors, found from southern China to Indonesia. Vietnamese tradition links the period to the kingdom of Văn Lang and its Hùng kings.

lead.en: The oldest known cemetery in the Pacific Islands

summary.en: In 2003 a cemetery of Vanuatu's first settlers, Lapita people who arrived about 3,000 years ago, was found near Teouma Bay on Efate. It is the oldest known cemetery in the Pacific Islands. Decorated Lapita pots lay with the dead, and many skeletons lacked their skulls, which seem to have been removed after burial.

lead.en: Stone heads of up to 40 tonnes, hauled 150 km

summary.en: The Olmecs carved giant heads up to 3.4 m tall and weighing from 5 to over 40 tonnes out of basalt boulders. The stone was hauled more than 150 km from the Tuxtla mountains, and each head has its own face and helmet: probably portraits of rulers.

lead.en: In the Bible, the central sanctuary of the worship of Yahweh

summary.en: According to the Bible, King Solomon built the First Temple in Jerusalem as the centre of the worship of Yahweh. No remains have been found, but it holds a central place in Jewish history and biblical tradition.

lead.en: A jaguar-god cult unites the Andes culturally

summary.en: In the Peruvian highlands, the temple centre of Chavín de Huántar arose with underground galleries and carved jaguar deities. Its religious style spread across the Andes, uniting a large region culturally.

lead.en: A clay pyramid and colossal heads on an island amid marshes

summary.en: After San Lorenzo declined, La Venta, on an island amid marshes near the Gulf of Mexico, became the main Olmec centre around 900–400 BC. Its builders raised a clay pyramid about 30 metres high, set up colossal stone heads and buried mosaic pavements of serpentine. Many of its monuments now stand in a park museum in Villahermosa.

lead.en: Nukuleka — the launch point for settling all of Polynesia

summary.en: Lapita voyagers landed on Tongatapu and founded Nukuleka, the oldest known settlement in Polynesia. From Tonga and Samoa their descendants would later settle the whole Polynesian Triangle.

title.en: Kalhu becomes the capital of Assyria

lead.en: Ashurnasirpal II opens his capital with a feast for 69,574

summary.en: Ashurnasirpal II moved the Assyrian capital to Kalhu and built a palace there with winged lamassu bulls and reliefs of his campaigns. According to the Banquet Stele, 69,574 guests attended the celebrations for the new capital in 879 BC. The ruins of Nimrud were badly damaged by Islamic State in 2015.

lead.en: Assyria against twelve kings, and the first mention of Arabs

summary.en: The Assyrian king Shalmaneser III met an alliance of twelve kings led by Hadadezer of Damascus on the Orontes. Among them were Ahab of Israel with 2,000 chariots and 'Gindibu the Arab' with 1,000 camels, the first mention of Arabs in history. The outcome was unclear, and the Assyrian advance stalled for a time.

lead.en: A revolt ousts King Li: the first firmly dated year in China

summary.en: The people of the Zhou capital rose against the harsh King Li, who fled. Until 828 BC regents governed — a period called Gonghe, 'joint harmony'. Sima Qian's chronological tables count years continuously from 841 BC, making it the first precisely dated year in Chinese history.

lead.en: By legend, Dido founds Rome's future great rival

summary.en: According to legend, Phoenicians from Tyre led by Princess Elissa (Dido) founded Carthage on the North African coast. It grew into the great sea power of the western Mediterranean and Rome's chief rival.

lead.en: Lapita sherds under water, the first trace of people on Samoa

summary.en: In 1973, dredging at the Mulifanua ferry berth on Upolu brought up thousands of Lapita pottery sherds. The now-submerged settlement is dated to around 800 BC, the oldest trace of people on Samoa. Samoa and Tonga later sent out the voyagers who settled all of Polynesia.

lead.en: The Urartian fortress from which Yerevan dates its history

summary.en: King Argishti I of Urartu built the fortress of Erebuni on the Arin Berd hill and recorded it in a cuneiform inscription. The fortress guarded Urartu's northern lands in the Ararat plain. Yerevan dates its history from it and celebrated its 2,800th anniversary in 2018.

lead.en: By tradition, the start of Greek dating by Olympiads

summary.en: The first recorded Olympic Games were held at the sanctuary of Zeus at Olympia; Coroebus of Elis won the stadion footrace. Held every four years, the Games gave the Greeks a common system for counting years.

lead.en: Nomads sack the capital, and the Zhou move east to Luoyi

summary.en: The Quanrong tribes, allied with disaffected nobles, took Haojing and killed King You. His heir moved the capital east to Luoyi (Luoyang). The Eastern Zhou kings became figureheads, and the Spring and Autumn period began, when rival states effectively ran the country.

lead.en: One eclipse record anchors the timeline of the ancient Near East

summary.en: Assyrian eponym lists recorded a solar eclipse in the month of Simanu, which astronomers identified as that of 15 June 763 BC. The entry became the anchor for the whole chronology of the ancient Near East.

lead.en: By legend, Romulus plants the seed of a future empire

summary.en: Roman tradition holds that Romulus founded the city on the Palatine Hill on 21 April 753 BC. Romans counted years 'from the founding of the City', and the small settlement grew into the centre of a vast empire.

lead.en: Troy and Odysseus' wanderings open European literature

summary.en: Tradition credits the poet Homer with the Iliad and the Odyssey, epics of the Trojan War and Odysseus's wanderings. They became the foundation of Greek education and the starting point of European literature.

lead.en: Nubian pharaohs take the throne and revive old traditions

summary.en: King Piye of Kush marched from Napata and conquered Egypt down to the Delta, founding the Twenty-fifth Dynasty. Nubian pharaohs ruled both kingdoms for about half a century and revived ancient Egyptian traditions.

lead.en: Per the chronicles, the start of an unbroken imperial line

summary.en: According to the Japanese chronicles Kojiki and Nihon Shoki, the legendary first emperor Jimmu ascended the throne at Kashihara. The date is mythical, but Japanese tradition counts its unbroken imperial line from it.

lead.en: Tens of thousands of tablets preserve the Epic of Gilgamesh

summary.en: The Assyrian king Ashurbanipal gathered tens of thousands of cuneiform tablets at Nineveh on religion, medicine, omens and literature. They preserved the Epic of Gilgamesh, the oldest great work of literature.

lead.en: Death for nearly every crime: the origin of 'draconian'

summary.en: Draco gave Athens its first written laws, replacing blood feuds with courts. Tradition says death was the penalty for almost any offence, and Solon later repealed everything except the homicide laws. Harsh rules have been called 'draconian' ever since.

lead.en: Babylon and Media bring the Assyrian empire to an end

summary.en: Babylonian and Median forces under Nabopolassar and Cyaxares captured and destroyed Nineveh, the Assyrian capital. Its fall ended the Assyrian Empire and opened the way for the rise of Neo-Babylonian power.

lead.en: Debt slavery abolished — a step toward Athenian democracy

summary.en: Elected archon, Solon abolished debt slavery, cancelled debts and divided citizens into property classes. His laws curbed the power of the aristocracy and laid the groundwork for Athenian democracy.

lead.en: The kingdom of Judah falls and the Babylonian exile begins

summary.en: After a long siege, the army of Nebuchadnezzar II of Babylon took Jerusalem and destroyed the First Temple. The Kingdom of Judah fell and much of its population was deported in the Babylonian exile, reshaping Judaism.

lead.en: The sun goes dark and Lydians and Medes make peace

summary.en: During a battle between Lydians and Medes near the Halys River on 28 May 585 BC, a total solar eclipse occurred, reportedly predicted by Thales of Miletus. Taking it as an omen, the two sides made peace.

lead.en: By tradition, the founder of Buddhism comes into the world

summary.en: By the traditional dating, Prince Siddhartha Gautama of the Shakya clan was born at Lumbini. After attaining enlightenment he became the Buddha and founded Buddhism, a world religion that spread across Asia.

lead.en: A teaching of virtue shapes China for two millennia

summary.en: Kong Qiu (Confucius) was born in the state of Lu. Teaching benevolence, filial piety and rule by virtue, he founded Confucianism, which shaped the state and society of China and East Asia for over two millennia.

title.en: Cyrus the Great founds the Achaemenid Empire

lead.en: Persia defeats Media and builds the era's largest empire

summary.en: The Persian king Cyrus II overthrew the Median king Astyages and founded the Achaemenid Empire. It soon became the largest empire of its time, from the Aegean to the Indus, known for tolerance and efficient administration.

lead.en: A colony of Miletus at the Bug estuary trades with the Scythians

summary.en: Settlers from Miletus founded Olbia, “the happy one”, on the Bug estuary, one of the first Greek cities on the northern Black Sea. It shipped grain, fish and slaves to Greece and sold wine, oil and painted pottery to the Scythians. Herodotus, who came here in the 5th century BC, described the Scythians around it. The city lasted about a thousand years; its ruins are a reserve near Parutyne in Ukraine’s Mykolaiv region.

title.en: Gold and silver coins of Croesus

lead.en: Pure gold and silver replace electrum — the first coin standard

summary.en: King Croesus of Lydia began striking coins of pure gold and silver at Sardis instead of earlier electrum pieces. They are regarded as the world's first standardised gold and silver coinage.

lead.en: The Neo-Babylonian kingdom ends and exiles return home

summary.en: The Persian army of Cyrus the Great took Babylon, ending the Neo-Babylonian Empire. Cyrus allowed deported peoples, including the Jews, to return home, a policy reflected in the Cyrus Cylinder.

title.en: Pythagoras founds his school at Croton

lead.en: Numbers as the essence of the cosmos — Greek math begins

summary.en: The philosopher Pythagoras of Samos settled at Croton in southern Italy and founded a religious and philosophical community. The Pythagoreans saw number as the basis of the cosmos and pioneered Greek mathematics and music theory.

lead.en: 50,000 Persian soldiers march into the desert and vanish

summary.en: According to Herodotus, Cambyses II sent 50,000 soldiers to subdue the oracle of Amun at the Siwa oasis. Halfway there a sandstorm engulfed them and they were never seen again. No trace has been found, and many historians consider the story a legend.

lead.en: Legend says the Persians used cats as shields against Egypt

summary.en: Cambyses’ victory at Pelusium gave Egypt to Persia. Seven centuries later the writer Polyaenus claimed that Cambyses placed cats and other sacred animals before his army, and the Egyptians dared not shoot.

lead.en: A trilingual cliff text that unlocked cuneiform

summary.en: Darius I had a relief and an account of his accession and victories over rebels carved on a cliff by the road from Mesopotamia to Media, in Old Persian, Elamite and Babylonian. In 1835–47 Henry Rawlinson copied it, and it became the key to deciphering cuneiform, as the Rosetta Stone was for hieroglyphs.

lead.en: By tradition, the kings are expelled and two consuls rule

summary.en: According to tradition, the Romans expelled their last king, Tarquin the Proud, and created a republic led by two annually elected consuls. The Republic lasted nearly five centuries and inspired modern political thought.

title.en: Cleisthenes' reforms and the birth of democracy

lead.en: Supreme power passes to the Athenian citizens' assembly

summary.en: Cleisthenes reorganised Athenian society into ten territorial tribes and gave the citizens' assembly supreme power. His reforms are regarded as the birth of democracy, government in which citizens themselves decide.

title.en: Sun Tzu's The Art of War

lead.en: 'All warfare is based on deception': the oldest book on strategy

summary.en: The 13-chapter treatise is attributed to Sun Tzu, a general of the state of Wu; most scholars think the text took shape in the 5th–4th centuries BC. Its core idea is that the best victory is won without battle, through cunning and knowing the enemy. Translated into French in 1772, it is still studied by soldiers and executives.

lead.en: A Carthaginian fleet sails past Gibraltar down Africa's coast

summary.en: The Carthaginian navigator Hanno led a fleet past the Pillars of Hercules and down the Atlantic coast of West Africa. His account, the Periplus, preserved in Greek translation, is one of the oldest descriptions of tropical Africa.

lead.en: The Zapotecs build a mountaintop capital that lasts 1,000 years

summary.en: The Zapotecs founded a city on a levelled mountaintop above the Valley of Oaxaca. Monte Albán remained their capital for over a thousand years and holds some of the earliest hieroglyphic and calendrical inscriptions in Mesoamerica.

title.en: Ancestral Polynesian homeland in Samoa and Tonga

lead.en: Lapita heirs become Polynesians, future settlers of Hawaii

summary.en: Descendants of the Lapita seafarers who settled Tonga and Samoa had by the mid-1st millennium BC forged a distinct Polynesian culture and language. From here, later voyagers in double canoes would settle East Polynesia, from Hawaii to New Zealand.

lead.en: Underground canals turn Fezzan's oases into a farming kingdom

summary.en: The Garamantes built a state with its capital at Garama in the Fezzan desert. Underground foggara canals brought ancient groundwater to their fields, and caravans linked the kingdom to the Mediterranean and the Sahel. Herodotus already described them; their kingdom declined as the water reserves ran out.

lead.en: The first great mound builders of the Ohio Valley

summary.en: The Adena people of the Ohio Valley raised earthen mounds over the graves of their elite; some, like Grave Creek in West Virginia, reached 20 metres. They grew squash and sunflowers and made copper ornaments and smoking pipes. Their traditions were carried on by the Hopewell culture.

lead.en: Asian Greeks defy Persia and spark the Persian Wars

summary.en: The Greek cities of Asia Minor, led by Miletus, rose against Persian rule; Athens and Eretria sent aid and the rebels burned Sardis. Persia crushed the revolt, sacking Miletus in 494 BC, and Athens' role gave Darius a reason to invade Greece.

lead.en: Athens first beats Persia and gives the marathon its name

summary.en: Athenian and Plataean hoplites under Miltiades defeated the Persian force Darius I had landed in Attica. The first major Greek victory over Persia boosted Athenian prestige and inspired the legend of the runner behind the modern marathon.

lead.en: Athenians vote with potsherds on whom to exile for 10 years

summary.en: Once a year Athenians could scratch the name of the most dangerous politician on a potsherd, an ostrakon; with a quorum of 6,000 votes he went into exile for ten years. The first victim was Hipparchus in 487 BC, and the word 'ostracism' lives on.

lead.en: By tradition, Gautama passes at Kushinagar; his teaching spreads

summary.en: Siddhartha Gautama, the Buddha, died at Kushinagar aged about 80; the date is debated, from c. 483 to c. 400 BC. His teaching on suffering and the path to liberation became Buddhism, which spread across Asia.

lead.en: Leonidas and his 300 Spartans hold the pass to the last man

summary.en: The Spartan king Leonidas and an allied Greek force held a narrow pass for three days against the vast army of Xerxes. When the Persians outflanked them by a mountain path, Leonidas and his 300 Spartans died, becoming a byword for self-sacrifice.

lead.en: Themistocles traps the Persian fleet in a narrow strait

summary.en: Following Themistocles' plan, the Greek fleet lured the Persian ships into the narrow strait off Salamis and destroyed them. Xerxes withdrew to Asia, and after Plataea in 479 BC the Persian invasion of Greece collapsed.

lead.en: A storm wrecks his bridges, so the king has the sea flogged

summary.en: Xerxes built two bridges across the Hellespont, but a storm destroyed them. According to Herodotus, the king had fetters thrown into the strait, the water given three hundred lashes and branded with hot irons. The new bridges were made of 674 ships tied together.

lead.en: China loses the teacher whose sayings will shape its state

summary.en: Confucius, a teacher who stressed filial piety, ritual and virtuous government, died in the state of Lu. His disciples compiled his sayings as the Analects; under the Han dynasty Confucianism became China's state ideology.

lead.en: A quake sparks a helot revolt and a rift with Athens

summary.en: A powerful earthquake devastated Sparta and, according to ancient sources, killed up to 20,000 people. The helots seized the moment to revolt, starting the Third Messenian War, which soured relations between Sparta and Athens.

lead.en: A dictator wins in 16 days and goes back to his farm

summary.en: Tradition says the Senate's envoys found Cincinnatus at his plough and made him dictator to rescue a trapped army. He beat the Aequi, laid down power after 16 days and went back to his farm, a model later invoked for George Washington.

lead.en: Pericles and Phidias crown the Acropolis with a masterpiece

summary.en: At Pericles' initiative a temple to Athena Parthenos rose on the Athenian Acropolis, designed by Ictinus and Callicrates with sculpture overseen by Phidias. The Parthenon became the high point of classical Greek architecture.

lead.en: Greek cities on the Kerch Strait feed Athens with grain

summary.en: The Greek colonies on both sides of the Kerch Strait united around Panticapaeum; in 438 BC power there passed to the Spartocid dynasty. The Bosporus shipped grain, fish and slaves to Athens, while Scythian and Maeotian nobles bought Greek gold and wine. The kingdom outlived the Hellenistic age and remained a Roman ally until the 4th century AD.

lead.en: Athens and Sparta exhaust each other; Athens surrenders

summary.en: The long war between Athens with its Delian League and Sparta with the Peloponnesian League ended in Athens' surrender in 404 BC. Chronicled by Thucydides, it exhausted the Greek city-states and broke Athenian power.

lead.en: Wartime epidemic kills up to a quarter of the city, Pericles too

summary.en: In the second year of the Peloponnesian War an epidemic struck refugee-packed Athens, killing perhaps a quarter of the population, Pericles among them. Thucydides, who survived it, described it in detail; the disease is still debated.

title.en: Cunaxa and the march of the Ten Thousand

lead.en: Greek mercenaries fight their way from Mesopotamia to the sea

summary.en: Cyrus the Younger and his Greek mercenaries marched against his brother, King Artaxerxes II, and Cyrus was killed at Cunaxa. The Ten Thousand Greeks, left without employer or generals, fought their way through the mountains of Kurdistan and Armenia to the Black Sea. One of them, Xenophon, told the story in the Anabasis.

lead.en: Permafrost kept the Altai nomads' carpets, felts and tattoos

summary.en: The nomads of the Pazyryk culture buried their elite in kurgans in the high Altai, where water seeped into the graves and froze. The permafrost preserved felt rugs, clothing, saddles, horse harness and tattooed bodies. The oldest known pile carpet, now in the Hermitage, comes from here.

lead.en: Athens condemns its philosopher; Plato makes him immortal

summary.en: An Athenian jury sentenced the philosopher Socrates to death for impiety and corrupting the youth; he drank hemlock. His pupil Plato immortalised him in dialogues, and the Socratic method became a foundation of Western philosophy.

lead.en: Guards and dogs slept through the Gauls; Juno's geese did not

summary.en: After the rout at the Allia the Gauls took Rome, and only the Capitol held out. According to Livy, the Gauls climbed the cliff at night unheard by sentries and dogs, but Juno's sacred geese raised the alarm and the former consul Marcus Manlius threw the attackers back.

lead.en: Legalist reforms turn Qin into the machine that will unite China

summary.en: From 356 BC Shang Yang, adviser to Duke Xiao of Qin, carried out Legalist reforms: ranks and land were granted for military merit, families were bound by collective responsibility, and uniform measures and counties run by officials were introduced. He was executed in 338 BC, but his system made Qin the strongest state and led to the unification of China.

title.en: Herostratus burns the Temple of Artemis

lead.en: He torched a world wonder for fame, so his name was banned

summary.en: Herostratus of Ephesus set fire to the Temple of Artemis, one of the Seven Wonders, and confessed under torture that he wanted eternal fame. The city banned his name on pain of death, but historians recorded it anyway, and 'Herostratic fame' became a byword.

lead.en: Darius III flees and the Persian Achaemenid empire collapses

summary.en: Alexander the Great routed the army of the Persian king Darius III, who fled the field. Babylon, Susa and Persepolis soon fell; the Achaemenid Empire collapsed and Alexander became master of an empire from Greece to India.

lead.en: Alexander plants the future capital of Hellenistic science

summary.en: Alexander the Great founded a city bearing his name on the Nile Delta coast. Under the Ptolemies Alexandria became Egypt's capital, the greatest port of the Mediterranean and the chief centre of Hellenistic learning.

lead.en: A Greek from Marseille first describes the midnight sun

summary.en: Around 325 BC Pytheas of Massalia sailed around Britain and on to mysterious Thule in the far north. He is the first person on record to describe the midnight sun and polar ice, and the first to link tides to the Moon; many contemporaries called him a liar.

lead.en: The conqueror leaves no heir; his generals carve up his world

summary.en: Alexander died in Babylon aged 32, leaving no capable heir. His generals, the Diadochi, carved up the empire into Hellenistic kingdoms — Ptolemaic, Seleucid, Antigonid — spreading Greek language and culture across the region.

lead.en: Chandragupta unites most of India for the first time

summary.en: Chandragupta Maurya, aided by his adviser Chanakya, overthrew the Nanda dynasty and took Pataliputra. He built the first empire to unite most of the Indian subcontinent.

lead.en: The only fully developed writing system of pre-Columbian America

summary.en: The oldest known Maya inscriptions, from San Bartolo, date to around the 3rd century BC. The script combined some 800 syllabic and word signs and could record any sentence of the language. The Spanish burned almost all Maya books; only four codices survive. The key to decipherment came in the 1950s from Soviet linguist Yuri Knorozov, who showed that the signs recorded sounds.

title.en: El Mirador, capital of the Preclassic Maya

lead.en: The Maya built giants centuries before Tikal

summary.en: In the jungle of northern Guatemala the city of El Mirador flourished from roughly the 3rd century BC to the 1st century AD. Its La Danta pyramid, about 70 metres high, is by volume one of the largest in the world, and paved causeways, the sacbeob, linked the city to its neighbours. Finds here overturned the view that complex Maya civilisation arose only in the Classic period; the city declined around AD 150.

lead.en: The Ptolemies try to collect every book in the known world

summary.en: Under the early Ptolemies the Mouseion and its library were founded in Alexandria, aiming to collect every book in the known world. Scholars such as Euclid and Eratosthenes worked there, and the library became a symbol of ancient learning.

lead.en: A 100-metre lighthouse that stood for over 1,500 years

summary.en: Under Ptolemy II a lighthouse at least 100 metres tall rose on the island of Pharos, for centuries one of the tallest structures on Earth. Only earthquakes between 956 and 1303 brought the wonder down, and the island's name became the word for lighthouse in many languages.

lead.en: 'One more such victory and we are undone'

summary.en: King Pyrrhus of Epirus and his elephants beat the Romans at Asculum but lost so many veterans that, according to Plutarch, he said one more such victory over the Romans would ruin him. A win that costs too much has been called Pyrrhic ever since.

title.en: Meroë becomes the heart of Kush

lead.en: Kush moves south to a city of pyramids and iron

summary.en: Around 270 BC the royal burials of Kush moved from Napata to Meroë on the Nile. The Meroitic kingdom, with its own script, pyramids and large-scale iron smelting, flourished until the 4th century AD.

lead.en: A bloody conquest turns Ashoka toward Buddhism

summary.en: Emperor Ashoka conquered Kalinga; by his own edict 100,000 were killed and 150,000 deported. Shaken by the bloodshed, Ashoka turned to Buddhism and proclaimed a policy of dhamma in edicts carved on rocks and pillars.

lead.en: Qin crushes Zhao and clears its path to supremacy

summary.en: The Qin army under Bai Qi encircled and destroyed the forces of Zhao; tradition says hundreds of thousands of surrendered soldiers were executed. One of the bloodiest battles of the Warring States, it cleared Qin's path to dominance.

lead.en: An early West African city with no palaces or foreign model

summary.en: The settlement in the Niger floodplain, 3 km from modern Djenné, arose around 250 BC. Excavations by Roderick and Susan McIntosh in 1977 and 1981 overturned the view that West African towns appeared only with Arab trade: by the 9th century it covered 33 hectares, smelted iron and traded in copper, gold and grain. Around 1400 the town was abandoned.

lead.en: Two shadows and geometry reveal the size of the planet

summary.en: Eratosthenes, head of the Library of Alexandria, compared noon shadows at Syene and Alexandria on the summer solstice and calculated the Earth's circumference. His result was remarkably close to the true value.

title.en: Earliest sure record of Halley's Comet

lead.en: Chinese chroniclers log it in the youth of the First Emperor

summary.en: Chinese chronicles preserved in Sima Qian's Records of the Grand Historian note a comet in 240 BC, the first reliable sighting of Halley's Comet. The state of Qin was then ruled by young Ying Zheng, the future First Emperor.

lead.en: The First Emperor imposes one script, one coin, one law

summary.en: After conquering Qi, the last rival state, King Ying Zheng of Qin took the title Shi Huangdi, 'First Emperor'. He standardised script, weights, coinage and law and began the Great Wall, creating a unified Chinese state.

lead.en: Elephants cross the mountains and bring war to Italy

summary.en: At the start of the Second Punic War the Carthaginian general Hannibal led an army with war elephants from Spain across the Alps into Italy. He lost nearly half his men but went on to crush the Romans at the Trebia, Lake Trasimene and Cannae.

lead.en: Hannibal's encirclement becomes the textbook battle

summary.en: Hannibal, who had crossed the Alps, encircled and annihilated a larger Roman army under the consuls Paullus and Varro. Cannae became the classic battle of encirclement, yet Rome refused to yield and fought on in the Second Punic War.

lead.en: Qin Shi Huang links old walls into one line against nomads

summary.en: Qin Shi Huang ordered the border walls of the former states joined into one line against the Xiongnu nomads, at the cost of tens of thousands of lives. Later dynasties, above all the Ming, rebuilt it, and with all its branches it exceeds 20,000 km.

lead.en: A giant claw lifted Roman ships out of the sea

summary.en: When Rome besieged Syracuse, the elderly Archimedes built defensive machines, among them the 'claw', a crane with a hook that lifted enemy ships and dropped them. The city held out for about two years; when it fell, a Roman soldier killed Archimedes without knowing who he was.

lead.en: Thousands of clay soldiers guard the First Emperor's tomb

summary.en: Qin Shi Huang died in 210 BC and was buried in a vast mausoleum at Mount Li. It is guarded by thousands of life-size clay warriors with horses and chariots, discovered by farmers in 1974.

title.en: Modu Chanyu builds the Xiongnu empire

lead.en: The first great nomad empire of the steppe challenges China

summary.en: Modu killed his father Touman and became chanyu of the Xiongnu. He crushed the Donghu and the Yuezhi and built an empire from Manchuria to the Tarim Basin. In 200 BC he surrounded the Han emperor Gaozu at Baideng, after which China paid off the Xiongnu for decades with tribute and princess brides.

lead.en: Liu Bang founds the dynasty that names the Chinese people

summary.en: After the fall of Qin and his victory over Xiang Yu, Liu Bang proclaimed himself emperor (Gaozu) with his capital at Chang'an. The Han ruled for over four centuries, and the Chinese still call themselves the Han people.

lead.en: Scipio defeats Hannibal and Rome rules the western sea

summary.en: The Roman general Scipio defeated Hannibal in North Africa. Under the peace of 201 BC Carthage lost its fleet and overseas lands, and Rome became the leading power of the western Mediterranean.

lead.en: The Xiongnu trap Liu Bang; Han pays tribute to the steppe

summary.en: The Xiongnu ruler Modu Chanyu surrounded the Han emperor Liu Bang near Pingcheng. After escaping, the Han adopted the heqin policy, sending princesses and tribute to the powerful Xiongnu steppe empire.

lead.en: Some of the ancient world's finest textiles, from Peru's desert

summary.en: In 1927 the Peruvian archaeologist Julio Tello discovered the Wari Kayan necropolis on the Paracas Peninsula, with more than 400 funerary bundles holding mummies. The bodies were wrapped in dozens of embroidered cotton and alpaca-wool mantles showing deities, animals and masked figures, made in the last centuries BC. The dry desert preserved their bright colours, and the Paracas culture was the forerunner of the Nazca.

title.en: The Memphis decree of the Rosetta Stone

lead.en: One decree in three scripts, the future key to hieroglyphs

summary.en: A synod of Egyptian priests at Memphis issued a decree honouring the young king Ptolemy V in hieroglyphs, Demotic and Greek. One copy, carved on a stele, was found by French soldiers near Rosetta in 1799. By comparing the texts, Jean-François Champollion deciphered Egyptian hieroglyphs in 1822.

lead.en: A mummy with soft skin and 138 melon seeds in her stomach

summary.en: Xin Zhui, wife of the Han Marquis of Dai, died around 168 BC. Her body, found in 1971, is one of the best-preserved mummies ever discovered. The autopsy found 138 melon seeds: she ate the melon a couple of hours before dying, so she died in summer.

lead.en: Rebels reclaim the Temple, the origin of Hanukkah

summary.en: The Seleucid king Antiochus IV banned Jewish rites and defiled the Temple in Jerusalem. The priest Mattathias and his sons, led by Judas Maccabeus, rose in revolt and freed Jerusalem in 164 BC. The rededication of the Temple is marked by Hanukkah, and the Hasmonean dynasty later built an independent Judean kingdom.

lead.en: A bronze 'computer' that predicted eclipses decades ahead

summary.en: In 1901 sponge divers raised a lump of geared bronze from a Roman-era shipwreck. It was a Greek device of the 2nd century BC that computed planetary positions, eclipses and even the years of the Olympic Games. Nothing as complex reappeared until the 14th century.

lead.en: Rome razes Carthage and stands without a rival

summary.en: After a three-year siege, Scipio Aemilianus took and razed Carthage, selling its survivors into slavery. Its land became the Roman province of Africa, leaving Rome the sole great power of the Mediterranean.

title.en: Zhang Qian's mission to the West

lead.en: An envoy survives captivity and opens China's road west

summary.en: Emperor Wu sent Zhang Qian to seek allies against the Xiongnu. After years in captivity he reached Ferghana and Bactria and returned with knowledge of the western lands. His journey opened China's way west — the future Silk Road.

lead.en: The start of a thousand years of Chinese rule in northern Vietnam

summary.en: Emperor Wu sent armies against Nanyue, a kingdom covering southern China and northern Vietnam. In 111 BC its capital Panyu fell and its lands became Han commanderies. For northern Vietnam it began more than a thousand years of Chinese rule, thrown off only in 938.

lead.en: China marches across Asia for a breed of horses

summary.en: Emperor Wu learned from Zhang Qian that Dayuan, in Fergana, bred swift 'heavenly horses'. When Dayuan refused to sell, a Han army twice crossed thousands of kilometres of desert, besieged its capital and came home with several thousand horses.

lead.en: Giant desert drawings whose purpose is still debated

summary.en: People of Peru's southern desert began creating giant geoglyphs on the plateau — straight lines, geometric shapes, and figures of a monkey, hummingbird and spider. Their purpose is still debated, most often linked to water and fertility rituals.

lead.en: An exchange network spanning half of North America

summary.en: From about 100 BC to AD 500 communities in the Ohio and Illinois valleys built huge geometric earthworks, circles, squares and octagons, some apparently aligned to moonrises. Their mounds hold obsidian from the Rocky Mountains, copper from the Great Lakes, shells from the Gulf of Mexico and mica from the Appalachians. Hopewell was not a state but a shared tradition of ritual and exchange.

title.en: Sima Qian's Records of the Grand Historian

lead.en: Sima Qian sets the model for all of China's official histories

summary.en: The court historian Sima Qian completed the Shiji, a 130-chapter history of China from the legendary Yellow Emperor to his own day. It became the model for all later official dynastic histories of China.

lead.en: A gladiator leads Italy's slaves against Rome

summary.en: In 73 BC some seventy slaves led by the Thracian Spartacus broke out of a gladiator school in Capua. His army grew to tens of thousands and defeated Roman legions for two years, until Crassus crushed it in 71 BC; six thousand captives were crucified along the Appian Way.

lead.en: Alesia wins Caesar the loyal army he turns on Rome

summary.en: In eight years Julius Caesar subdued Gaul, roughly modern France and Belgium; the decisive moment was the siege of Alesia in 52 BC, where Vercingetorix surrendered. The conquest gave Caesar wealth and a loyal army with which he soon seized power in Rome.

lead.en: Parthian archers destroy Crassus and halt Rome's eastward push

summary.en: Parthian cavalry under Surena — horse archers and cataphracts — crushed the Roman legions of Marcus Crassus, who was killed. The defeat halted Rome's eastward expansion and made Parthia its chief rival.

lead.en: To launch his calendar, Caesar made one year 445 days long

summary.en: Rome's calendar had drifted so far from the Sun that Julius Caesar, introducing a new one, made 46 BC 445 days long, nicknamed the 'last year of confusion'. The Julian calendar began in 45 BC, and the Russian and several other Orthodox churches still use it.

lead.en: Senators kill the dictator and doom the Republic instead

summary.en: On the Ides of March, senators led by Brutus and Cassius stabbed the dictator Julius Caesar to death at a Senate meeting in the Curia of Pompey. Instead of saving the Republic, the murder unleashed new civil wars that brought Octavian to power.

lead.en: First record of the calendar the Maya would later use

summary.en: Stela 2 at Chiapa de Corzo bears the date 7.16.3.2.13 — December 36 BC, the oldest known Mesoamerican Long Count inscription. The calendar, later used by the Maya, counted days from a mythical starting point in 3114 BC.

lead.en: Octavian beats Antony and Cleopatra and takes Egypt

summary.en: Octavian's fleet under Agrippa defeated the navy of Mark Antony and Cleopatra of Egypt. Within a year both had taken their own lives, Egypt became a Roman province and Octavian the sole ruler of the Roman world.

lead.en: Egypt falls to Rome and the Ptolemaic line ends

summary.en: After the defeat at Actium and Mark Antony's suicide, the last Ptolemaic queen took her own life as Octavian entered Alexandria. Egypt became a Roman province, ending the age of the Hellenistic kingdoms.

lead.en: The Republic keeps its facade as the Roman Empire is born

summary.en: The Senate granted Octavian the honorific name Augustus. Keeping republican forms while holding real power, he created the Principate; the year is conventionally taken as the start of the Roman Empire and the Pax Romana.

title.en: Augustus's head under the steps at Meroë

lead.en: Kush buried the emperor's head beneath a temple stair

summary.en: The army of Queen Amanirenas of Kush raided Roman Egypt and smashed statues of Augustus. One bronze head was taken to Meroë and buried under the steps of a temple, apparently to be walked over. It was dug up in 1910 and is now in the British Museum.

lead.en: The Gospel story behind the Anno Domini calendar

summary.en: According to the Gospels, Jesus was born in Bethlehem during the reign of King Herod. In the 6th century the monk Dionysius Exiguus made it the starting point of the Anno Domini era, though historians place the birth around 6–4 BC.
